**Stephen Grover Cleveland** (March 18, 1837–June 24, 1908) was the 22nd and 24th [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), serving from 1885 to 1889 and from 1893 to 1897. He was the first [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Democratic_Party_(United_States) "History of the Democratic Party (United States)") elected president after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") and the first U.S. president to serve nonconsecutive terms.

Born in [Caldwell, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldwell,_New_Jersey "Caldwell, New Jersey"), Cleveland was elected [mayor of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Buffalo "Mayor of Buffalo") in 1881 and [governor of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York") in 1882. While governor, he closely cooperated with [state assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Assembly "New York State Assembly") minority leader [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") to pass reform measures, winning national attention.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:2-2) He led the [Bourbon Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourbon_Democrats "Bourbon Democrats"), a pro-business movement opposed to [high tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_tariffs_in_the_United_States#Civil_War "History of tariffs in the United States"), [free silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_silver "Free silver"), [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation"), [imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism"), and [subsidies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidies "Subsidies") to businesses, farmers, or veterans. His crusade for political reform and [fiscal conservatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_conservatism "Fiscal conservatism") made him an icon for American conservatives of the time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-3) Cleveland also won praise for honesty, self-reliance, integrity, and commitment to [classical liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_liberalism "Classical liberalism").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-4) His fight against political corruption, patronage, and [bossism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossism "Bossism") convinced many like-minded Republicans, called "[Mugwumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugwumps "Mugwumps")", to cross party lines and support him in the [1884 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election "1884 United States presidential election"), which he narrowly won against Republican [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine").

During [his first presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Grover_Cleveland "First presidency of Grover Cleveland"), Cleveland signed the [Interstate Commerce Act of 1887](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Act_of_1887 "Interstate Commerce Act of 1887"), which made the [railroad industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport "Rail transport") the first industry subject to federal regulation by a regulatory body,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-NatArchive2021-5) and the [Dawes Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Act "Dawes Act"), which subdivided [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribal communal landholdings into individual allotments. This policy led to Native Americans ceding control of about two-thirds of their land between 1887 and 1934.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:7-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:8-7) In the [1888 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1888_United_States_presidential_election "1888 United States presidential election"), Cleveland won the [popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_vote "Popular vote") but lost the [electoral college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") and therefore the election to [Benjamin Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison "Benjamin Harrison"). He returned to New York City and joined a [law firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_firm "Law firm").

In a rematch against Harrison for the [1892 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1892_United_States_presidential_election "1892 United States presidential election"), Cleveland won both the popular vote and electoral college, returning him to the White House. One month before [his second presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Grover_Cleveland "Second presidency of Grover Cleveland") began, the [Panic of 1893](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1893 "Panic of 1893") sparked a severe national depression. An [anti-imperialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-imperialism "Anti-imperialism"), Cleveland opposed the push to [annex Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Hawaii#End_and_annexation_of_the_Republic "Republic of Hawaii"), launched [an investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blount_Report "Blount Report") into [the 1893 coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overthrow_of_the_Hawaiian_Kingdom "Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom") against Queen [Liliʻuokalani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lili%CA%BBuokalani "Liliʻuokalani"), and called for her restoration.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:4-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:5-9) Cleveland intervened in the 1894 [Pullman Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_Strike "Pullman Strike") to keep the railroads moving, angering [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") Democrats and [labor unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_history_of_the_United_States "Labor history of the United States") nationwide; his support of the [gold standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard "Gold standard") and opposition to free silver alienated the [agrarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrarianism "Agrarianism") wing of the Democrats.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-tugwell-10) Critics complained that Cleveland had little imagination and seemed overwhelmed by the nation's economic disasters—[depressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_depression "Economic depression") and [strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_US_strikes_by_size "List of US strikes by size")—in his second term.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-tugwell-10) Many voters blamed the Democrats, opening the way for a [Republican landslide in 1894](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1894_United_States_House_elections "1894 United States House elections") and for the agrarian and free silver (silverite) seizure of the Democratic Party at the [1896 Democratic convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Democratic_National_Convention "1896 Democratic National Convention"). By the end of his second term, he was highly unpopular, even among Democrats.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-11)

After leaving the White House, Cleveland served as a trustee of [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"). He joined the [American Anti-Imperialist League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Anti-Imperialist_League "American Anti-Imperialist League") in protest of the 1898 [Spanish–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War "Spanish–American War").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:3-12) He died in 1908.

Stephen Grover Cleveland was born on March 18, 1837, in [Caldwell, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldwell,_New_Jersey "Caldwell, New Jersey"), to Ann (née Neal) and [Richard Falley Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Falley_Cleveland "Richard Falley Cleveland").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-13) Cleveland's father, originally from [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut"), was a [Congregational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalism_in_the_United_States "Congregationalism in the United States") and [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism_in_the_United_States "Presbyterianism in the United States") minister.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-14) His mother was from [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore") and was the daughter of a bookseller.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-15) On his father's side, Cleveland was descended from English ancestors who first emigrated to [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") from [Ipswich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich,_England "Ipswich, England"), England, in 1635.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-16) On his mother's side, Cleveland was descended from Anglo-Irish Protestants and German [Quakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-17) Cleveland was distantly related to General [Moses Cleaveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Cleaveland "Moses Cleaveland"), after whom the city of [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio, was named.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-18)

Cleveland, the fifth of nine children, was named Stephen Grover in honor of the first pastor of the First Presbyterian Church of Caldwell, where his father was pastor at the time. He became known as Grover in his adult life.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-19) In 1841, the Cleveland family moved to [Fayetteville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayetteville,_New_York "Fayetteville, New York"), where Grover spent much of his childhood.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-20) Neighbors later described him as "full of fun and inclined to play pranks",[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-21) and fond of outdoor sports.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-22)

In 1850, Cleveland's father Richard moved his family to [Clinton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Oneida_County,_New_York "Clinton, Oneida County, New York"), accepting a job there as district secretary for the [American Home Missionary Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Home_Missionary_Society "American Home Missionary Society").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-23) Despite his father's dedication to his missionary work, his income was insufficient for the large family. Financial conditions forced him to remove Grover from school and place him in a two-year mercantile apprenticeship in Fayetteville. The experience was valuable, though brief. Grover returned to Clinton and his schooling at the completion of the apprentice contract.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-24) In 1853, missionary work began to take a toll on Richard's health. He took a new work assignment in [Holland Patent, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Patent,_New_York "Holland Patent, New York"), and moved his family once again.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins21-25) Shortly after, Richard Cleveland died from a [gastric ulcer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastric_ulcer "Gastric ulcer"). Grover was said to have learned about his father's death from a boy selling newspapers.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins21-25)

### Education and moving west

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Grover_Cleveland_young_photo.jpg/250px-Grover_Cleveland_young_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grover_Cleveland_young_photo.jpg)

Early and undated photograph of Cleveland

Cleveland received his elementary education at the Fayetteville Academy and the [Clinton Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Oneida_County,_New_York#History_of_education "Clinton, Oneida County, New York") (not to be confused with the Clinton Liberal Institute).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-26) After his father died in 1853, he again left school to help support his family. Later that year, Cleveland's brother William was hired as a teacher at the [New York Institute for the Blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Institute_for_the_Blind "New York Institute for the Blind") in New York City, and William obtained a place for Cleveland as an assistant teacher. Cleveland returned home to Holland Patent at the end of 1854, where an elder in his church offered to pay for his college education if he promised to become a minister. Cleveland declined, and in 1855 he decided to move west.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-27)

He stopped first in [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York"), where his cousin [Lewis F. Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_F._Allen "Lewis F. Allen") gave him a clerical job.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-28) Allen was an important man in Buffalo, and he introduced Cleveland to influential men there, including the partners in the [law firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_firm "Law firm") of Rogers, Bowen, and Rogers.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-29) Cleveland later took a clerkship with the firm, began to [read the law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read_the_law "Read the law") with them, and was admitted to the [New York bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_examination_in_the_United_States "Bar examination in the United States") in 1859.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff14-30)

### Early career and the American Civil War

Cleveland worked for the Rogers firm for three years before leaving in 1862 to start his own practice.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-31) In January 1863, he was appointed assistant [district attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_attorney "District attorney") of [Erie County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_County,_New_York "Erie County, New York").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-32) With the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") raging, Congress passed the [Conscription Act of 1863](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_Act_of_1863 "Conscription Act of 1863"), requiring able-bodied men to serve in the army if called upon, or else to hire a substitute.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff14-30) Cleveland chose the latter, paying $150, equivalent to $3,922 in 2025, to [George Brinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Brinski "George Brinski"), a [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") immigrant, to serve in his place.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-33)

As a lawyer, Cleveland became known for his single-minded concentration and dedication to hard work.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins52-34) In 1866, he successfully defended some participants in the [Fenian raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenian_raids#Canada_West "Fenian raids"), working _[pro bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro\_bono "Pro bono")_ (free of charge).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-35) In 1868, Cleveland attracted professional attention for his winning defense of a [libel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libel "Libel") suit against the editor of Buffalo's _Commercial Advertiser_.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-36) During this time, Cleveland assumed a lifestyle of simplicity, taking residence in a plain [boarding house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_house "Boarding house"). He devoted his growing income to the support of his mother and younger sisters.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-37) While his personal quarters were austere, Cleveland enjoyed an active social life and "the easy-going sociability of hotel-lobbies and [saloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_saloon "Western saloon")".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-38) He shunned the circles of higher society of Buffalo in which his uncle-in-law's family traveled.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-39)

## Political career in New York

### Sheriff of Erie County

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/DSCN4468_buffaloclevelandstatue_e.jpg/250px-DSCN4468_buffaloclevelandstatue_e.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DSCN4468_buffaloclevelandstatue_e.jpg)

A statue of Grover Cleveland outside [City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_City_Hall "Buffalo City Hall") in [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York")

From his earliest involvement in politics, Cleveland aligned with the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-40) He had a decided aversion to Republicans [John C. Frémont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont "John C. Frémont") and [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln"), and the heads of the Rogers law firm were solid Democrats.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-41) In 1865, he ran for [District Attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Attorney "District Attorney"), losing narrowly to his friend and roommate, [Lyman K. Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyman_K._Bass "Lyman K. Bass"), the Republican nominee.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins52-34)

In 1870, with the help of friend Oscar Folsom, Cleveland secured the Democratic nomination for [sheriff of Erie County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheriff_of_Erie_County,_New_York "Sheriff of Erie County, New York").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins58-42) He won the election by a 303-vote margin and took office on January 1, 1871, at age 33.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-44) While this new career took him away from the practice of law, it was rewarding in other ways: the fees were said to yield up to $40,000, equivalent to $1,075,000 in 2025, over the two-year term.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins58-42)

Cleveland's service as sheriff was unremarkable. Biographer [Rexford Tugwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rexford_Tugwell "Rexford Tugwell") described the time in office as a waste for Cleveland politically. Cleveland was aware of graft in the sheriff's office during his tenure and chose not to confront it.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-45) A notable incident of his term took place on September 6, 1872, when Patrick Morrissey was executed. He had been convicted of murdering his mother.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-morrisey-46) As sheriff, Cleveland was responsible for either personally carrying out the execution or paying a deputy $10 to perform the task.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-morrisey-46) In spite of reservations about the hanging, Cleveland executed Morrissey himself.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-morrisey-46) He hanged another murderer, [John Gaffney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_executed_in_New_York "List of people executed in New York"), on February 14, 1873.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-47)

After his term as sheriff ended, Cleveland returned to his law practice, opening a firm with his friends Lyman K. Bass and [Wilson S. Bissell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_S._Bissell "Wilson S. Bissell").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-48) Bass was later replaced by [George J. Sicard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_J._Sicard "George J. Sicard").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-locTimeline-49) Elected to Congress in 1872, Bass did not spend much time at the firm, but Cleveland and Bissell soon rose to the top of Buffalo's legal community.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-50) Up to that point, Cleveland's political career had been honorable and unexceptional. As biographer [Allan Nevins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Nevins "Allan Nevins") wrote, "Probably no man in the country, on March 4, 1881, had less thought than this limited, simple, sturdy attorney of Buffalo that four years later he would be standing in [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") and taking the oath as President of the United States."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-51)

It was during this period that Cleveland began courting a widow, [Maria Halpin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Halpin "Maria Halpin"). She later accused him of raping her.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:9-54) It is unclear if Halpin was actually raped by Cleveland or if their relationship was consensual.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:0-55) In March 1876, Cleveland accused Halpin of being an alcoholic and had her child removed from her custody. The child was taken to the [Protestant Orphan Asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Orphans'_Asylum "Protestant Orphans' Asylum"), and Cleveland paid for his stay there.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:0-55) Cleveland had Halpin admitted to the Providence Asylum. Halpin was only kept at the asylum for five days because she was deemed not to be insane.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:0-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-56) Cleveland later provided financial support for her to begin her own business outside of Buffalo.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:0-55) Although lacking irrefutable evidence that Cleveland was the father,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:1-57) the child became a campaign issue for the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Republican_Party_(United_States) "History of the Republican Party (United States)") in Cleveland's first presidential campaign, where they smeared him by claiming that he was "immoral" and for allegedly acting cruelly by not raising the child himself.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:1-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-Henry_F._Graff_2002_61%E2%80%9363-58)

### Mayor of Buffalo

In the 1870s, the municipal government in Buffalo had grown increasingly corrupt, with Democratic and Republican [political machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machine "Political machine") cooperating to share the [spoils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoils_system "Spoils system") of political office.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-59) When the Republicans nominated a slate of particularly disreputable machine politicians for the 1881 election, Democrats saw an opportunity to gain the votes of disaffected Republicans by nominating a more honest candidate.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-60) Party leaders approached Cleveland, who agreed to run for [Mayor of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Buffalo,_New_York "List of mayors of Buffalo, New York") provided the party's slate of candidates for other offices was to his liking.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins80-61) More notorious politicians were left off the Democratic ticket and he accepted the nomination.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins80-61) Cleveland [was elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1881_Buffalo_mayoral_election "1881 Buffalo mayoral election") mayor that November with 15,120 votes, while his Republican opponent [Milton Earl Beebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Earl_Beebe "Milton Earl Beebe") received 11,528 votes.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-62) He took office on January 2, 1882.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-LOC-Timeline-63)

Cleveland's term as mayor was spent fighting the entrenched interests of the party machines.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-64) Among the acts that established his reputation was a veto of the street-cleaning bill passed by the [Buffalo Common Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Common_Council "Buffalo Common Council").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-street-65) The street-cleaning contract had been the subject of competitive bidding, and the Council selected the highest bidder at $422,000, rather than the lowest at $100,000 less, because of the political connections of the bidder.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-street-65) Previous mayors had allowed similar bills in the past, but Cleveland's veto message said, "I regard it as the culmination of a most bare-faced, impudent, and shameless scheme to betray the interests of the people, and to worse than squander the public money."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-66) The Council reversed itself and awarded the contract to the lowest bidder.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-67) Cleveland also asked the state legislature to form a Commission to develop a plan to improve the sewer system in Buffalo at a much lower cost than previously proposed locally; this plan was successfully adopted.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-68) For this, and other actions safeguarding public funds, Cleveland began to gain a reputation beyond Erie County as a leader willing to purge government corruption.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-69)

### Governor of New York

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/GCleveland.png/250px-GCleveland.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GCleveland.png)

Gubernatorial portrait of Grover Cleveland

Democratic party officials started to consider Cleveland a possible nominee for [Governor of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins94-70)[Daniel Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Manning "Daniel Manning"), a party insider who admired Cleveland's record, was instrumental in his candidacy.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-71) With a split in the state Republican Party in 1882, the Democratic party was considered to be at an advantage; several men contended for that party's nomination.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins94-70) The two leading Democratic candidates were [Roswell P. Flower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_P._Flower "Roswell P. Flower") and [Henry Warner Slocum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Warner_Slocum "Henry Warner Slocum"). Their factions deadlocked and the convention could not agree on a nominee.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-72) Cleveland, who came in third place on the first ballot, picked up support in subsequent votes and emerged as the compromise choice.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-73) With Republicans still divided heading into [the general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1882_New_York_state_election "1882 New York state election"), Cleveland emerged the victor, receiving 535,318 votes to Republican nominee [Charles J. Folger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_J._Folger "Charles J. Folger")'s 342,464.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-74) Cleveland's margin of victory was, at the time, the largest in a contested New York election. The Democrats also picked up seats in both houses of the [New York State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-75)

Cleveland brought his opposition to needless spending to the governor's office. He promptly sent the legislature eight vetoes in his first two months in office.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-76) The first to attract attention was his veto of a bill to reduce the fares on [New York City elevated trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_New_York_City_Subway#Steam_railways "History of the New York City Subway") to five cents.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-77) The bill had broad support because the trains' owner, [Jay Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Gould "Jay Gould"), was unpopular, and his fare increases were widely denounced.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-78) Cleveland saw the bill as unjust—Gould had taken over the railroads when they were failing and had made the system solvent again.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins116-79) Cleveland believed that altering Gould's franchise would violate the [Contract Clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_Clause "Contract Clause") of the [federal Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins116-79) Despite the initial popularity of the fare-reduction bill, the newspapers praised Cleveland's veto.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins116-79)[Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt"), then a member of the [Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Assembly "New York State Assembly"), had reluctantly voted for the bill with the intention of holding railroad barons accountable.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins117-80) After the veto, Roosevelt and other legislators reversed their position, and Cleveland's veto was sustained.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins117-80)

Cleveland's defiance of political corruption won him popular acclaim; it also brought the enmity of New York City's influential [Tammany Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammany_Hall "Tammany Hall") organization and its boss, [John Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kelly_(New_York_politician) "John Kelly (New York politician)").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-81) Tammany Hall and Kelly had disapproved of Cleveland's nomination for governor, and their resistance intensified after Cleveland openly opposed and prevented the reelection of [Thomas F. Grady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_F._Grady "Thomas F. Grady"), their point man in the State Senate.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-82) Cleveland also steadfastly opposed other Tammany nominees, as well as bills passed as a result of their deal-making.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-83) The loss of Tammany's support was offset by the support of Theodore Roosevelt and other reform-minded Republicans, who helped Cleveland pass several laws to reform municipal governments.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-84) Cleveland closely worked with Roosevelt, who served as assembly minority leader in 1883; the municipal legislation they cooperated on gained Cleveland national recognition.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:2-2)

## 1884 Presidential Election

Main articles: [1884 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election "1884 United States presidential election") and [Grover Cleveland 1884 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland_1884_presidential_campaign "Grover Cleveland 1884 presidential campaign")

### Nomination for president

Main article: [1884 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_Democratic_National_Convention "1884 Democratic National Convention")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Bernard_Gilliam_-_Phryne_before_the_Chicago_Tribunal.jpg/330px-Bernard_Gilliam_-_Phryne_before_the_Chicago_Tribunal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bernard_Gilliam_-_Phryne_before_the_Chicago_Tribunal.jpg)

An anti-Blaine cartoon presents him as the "tattooed man", with many indelible scandals.

In June 1884, the Republican Party convened their [national convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_Republican_National_Convention "1884 Republican National Convention") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), selecting former U.S. House Speaker [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") as their nominee for president. Blaine's nomination alienated many Republicans, including the [Mugwumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugwumps "Mugwumps"), who viewed Blaine as ambitious and immoral.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins185-85) The Republican standard-bearer was further weakened when the Conkling faction and President [Chester Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Arthur "Chester Arthur") refused to give Blaine their strong support.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-86) Democratic party leaders believed the Republicans' choice gave them an opportunity to win the White House for the first time since 1856 if the right candidate could be found.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins185-85)

Among the Democrats, [Samuel J. Tilden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_J._Tilden "Samuel J. Tilden") was the initial front-runner, having been the party's nominee in the [contested election of 1876](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_United_States_presidential_election "1876 United States presidential election").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins146-87) After Tilden declined a nomination due to his poor health, his supporters shifted to several other contenders.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins146-87) Cleveland was among the leaders in early support, and [Thomas F. Bayard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_F._Bayard "Thomas F. Bayard") of [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware"), [Allen G. Thurman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_G._Thurman "Allen G. Thurman") of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), [Samuel Freeman Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Freeman_Miller "Samuel Freeman Miller") of [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), and [Benjamin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Butler_(politician) "Benjamin Butler (politician)") of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") also had considerable followings, along with various [favorite sons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favorite_son "Favorite son").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins146-87) Each of the other candidates had hindrances to his nomination: Bayard had spoken in favor of [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") in 1861, making him unacceptable to Northerners; Butler, conversely, was reviled throughout the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") for his actions during the American Civil War; Thurman was generally well-liked, but was growing old and infirm, and his views on the [silver question](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimetallism "Bimetallism") were uncertain.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-88)

Cleveland, too, had detractors—Tammany remained opposed to him—but the nature of his enemies made him still more friends.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-89) Cleveland led on the first ballot, with 392 votes out of 820.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-90) On the second ballot, Tammany threw its support behind Butler, but the rest of the delegates shifted to Cleveland, who won. Thomas A. Hendricks of [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") was selected as his running mate.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins154-91)

### Campaign against Blaine

Corruption in politics was the central issue in 1884; Blaine had over the span of his career been involved in several questionable deals.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-92) Cleveland's reputation as an opponent of corruption proved the Democrats' strongest asset.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-93) William C. Hudson created Cleveland's contextual campaign slogan "A public office is a public trust."[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-94) Reform-minded Republicans called "[Mugwumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugwump "Mugwump")" denounced Blaine as corrupt and flocked to Cleveland.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-mugwump-95) The Mugwumps, including such men as [Carl Schurz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Schurz "Carl Schurz") and [Henry Ward Beecher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ward_Beecher "Henry Ward Beecher"), were more concerned with morality than with party, and felt Cleveland was a kindred soul who would promote civil service reform and fight for efficiency in government.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-mugwump-95) At the same time that the Democrats gained support from the Mugwumps, they lost some blue-collar workers to the [Greenback-Labor party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Greenback_Party "United States Greenback Party"), led by ex-Democrat Benjamin Butler.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-96) In general, Cleveland abided by the precedent of minimizing presidential campaign travel and speechmaking; Blaine became one of the first to break with that tradition.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-97)

The campaign focused on the candidates' moral standards, as each side cast aspersions on their opponents. Cleveland's supporters rehashed the old allegations that Blaine had corruptly influenced legislation in favor of the [Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock_and_Fort_Smith_Railroad "Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad") and the [Union Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railway "Union Pacific Railway"), later profiting on the sale of bonds he owned in both companies.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-blaine-98) Although the stories of Blaine's favors to the railroads had made the rounds eight years earlier, this time Blaine's correspondence was discovered, making his earlier denials less plausible.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-blaine-98) On some of the most damaging correspondence, Blaine had written "Burn this letter", giving Democrats the last line to their rallying cry: "Blaine, Blaine, James G. Blaine, the continental liar from the state of Maine, 'Burn this letter!'"[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-99)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Another_voice_for_Cleveland_-_F.B._LCCN95522869_-_restoration2.jpg/250px-Another_voice_for_Cleveland_-_F.B._LCCN95522869_-_restoration2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Another_voice_for_Cleveland_-_F.B._LCCN95522869_-_restoration2.jpg)

An anti-Cleveland cartoon highlights the Halpin scandal.

Regarding Cleveland, commentator [Jeff Jacoby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Jacoby_(columnist) "Jeff Jacoby (columnist)") notes that, "Not since George Washington had a candidate for President been so renowned for his rectitude."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-100) But the Republicans found a refutation buried in Cleveland's past. Aided by the sermons of Reverend [George H. Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._Ball "George H. Ball"), a minister from Buffalo, they made public the allegation that Cleveland had fathered a child while he was a lawyer there,[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-101) and their rallies soon included the chant "Ma, Ma, where's my Pa?".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-102) When confronted with the scandal, Cleveland immediately instructed his supporters to "Above all, tell the truth."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-Henry_F._Graff_2002_61%E2%80%9363-58) He admitted to paying child support in 1874 to Maria Crofts Halpin, the woman who asserted he had fathered her son Oscar Folsom Cleveland and he assumed responsibility.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-Henry_F._Graff_2002_61%E2%80%9363-58) Shortly before the [1884 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election "1884 United States presidential election"), the Republican media published an affidavit from Halpin in which she stated that until she met Cleveland, her "life was pure and spotless", and "there is not, and never was, a doubt as to the paternity of our child, and the attempt of Grover Cleveland, or his friends, to couple the name of Oscar Folsom, or any one else, with that boy, for that purpose is simply infamous and false."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-103)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/ElectoralCollege1884.svg/500px-ElectoralCollege1884.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1884.svg)

The results of [the 1884 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_United_States_presidential_election "1884 United States presidential election")

The electoral votes of closely contested New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Connecticut would determine the election.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-104) In New York, the Tammany Democrats decided that they would gain more from supporting a Democrat they disliked than a Republican who would do nothing for them.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-105) Blaine hoped that he would have more support from Irish Americans than Republicans typically did; while the Irish were mainly a Democratic constituency in the 19th century, Blaine's mother was Irish Catholic, and he had been supportive of the [Irish National Land League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_National_Land_League "Irish National Land League") while he was Secretary of State.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-106) The Irish, a significant group in three of the [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state"), did appear inclined to support Blaine until a Republican, [Samuel D. Burchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_D._Burchard_(clergyman) "Samuel D. Burchard (clergyman)"), gave a speech pivotal for the Democrats, denouncing them as the party of "Rum, [Romanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanism "Romanism"), and Rebellion".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-107) The Democrats spread the word of this implied anti-Catholic insult on the eve of the election. They also blistered Blaine for attending a banquet with some of New York City's wealthiest men.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-108)

After the votes were counted, Cleveland narrowly won all four of the swing states, including New York by 1,200 votes.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-leip1884-109) While the popular vote total was close, with Cleveland winning by just one-quarter of a percent, the electoral votes gave Cleveland a majority of 219–182.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-leip1884-109) Following the electoral victory, the "Ma, Ma..." attack phrase gained a classic riposte: "Gone to the White House. Ha! Ha! Ha!"[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-110)

## First presidency (1885–1889)

Main article: [First presidency of Grover Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Grover_Cleveland "First presidency of Grover Cleveland")

### Reform

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Cleveland_Tariffs_%28edit%29.jpg/330px-Cleveland_Tariffs_%28edit%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cleveland_Tariffs_(edit).jpg)

Cleveland portrayed as a tariff reformer

Soon after taking office, Cleveland was faced with the task of filling all the government jobs for which the president had the power of appointment. These jobs were typically filled under the [spoils system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoils_system "Spoils system"), but Cleveland announced that he would not fire any Republican who was doing his job well, and would not appoint anyone solely on the basis of party service.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-111) He also used his appointment powers to reduce the number of federal employees, as many departments had become bloated with political time-servers.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-112) Later in his term, as his fellow Democrats chafed at being excluded from the spoils, Cleveland began to replace more of the partisan Republican officeholders with Democrats;[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-113) this was especially the case with policymaking positions.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-114) While some of his decisions were influenced by party concerns, more of Cleveland's appointments were decided by merit alone than was the case in his predecessors' administrations.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-115)

Cleveland also reformed other parts of the government. In 1887, he signed an act creating the [Interstate Commerce Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission "Interstate Commerce Commission").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-116) He and [Secretary of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Navy "Secretary of the Navy")[William C. Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._Whitney "William C. Whitney") undertook to modernize the [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") and canceled construction contracts that had resulted in inferior ships.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-117) Cleveland angered railroad investors by ordering an investigation of Western lands they held by government grant. [Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior")[Lucius Q. C. Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Q._C._Lamar "Lucius Q. C. Lamar") charged that the rights of way for this land must be returned to the public because the railroads failed to extend their lines according to agreements. The lands were forfeited, resulting in the return of approximately 81,000,000 acres (330,000 km 2).[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-rrgrants-118)

Cleveland was the first Democratic president subject to the [Tenure of Office Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenure_of_Office_Act_(1867) "Tenure of Office Act (1867)") which originated in 1867; the act purported to require the Senate to approve the dismissal of any presidential appointee who was originally subject to its advice and consent. Cleveland objected to the act in principle and his steadfast refusal to abide by it prompted its fall into disfavor and led to its ultimate repeal in 1887.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-119)

### Vetoes

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/CLEVELAND%2C_Grover-President_%28BEP_engraved_portrait%29.jpg/330px-CLEVELAND%2C_Grover-President_%28BEP_engraved_portrait%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CLEVELAND,_Grover-President_(BEP_engraved_portrait).jpg)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CLEVELAND,_Grover-President_(BEP_engraved_portrait).jpg "File:CLEVELAND, Grover-President (BEP engraved portrait).jpg")

[Bureau of Engraving and Printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Engraving_and_Printing "Bureau of Engraving and Printing") (BEP) engraved portrait of Cleveland as president 

As Congress and its Republican-led Senate sent Cleveland legislation he opposed, he often resorted to using his veto power.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-120) He vetoed hundreds of private pension bills for American Civil War veterans, believing that if their pensions requests had already been rejected by the [Pension Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension_Bureau "Pension Bureau"), Congress should not attempt to override that decision.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-121) When Congress, pressured by the [Grand Army of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Army_of_the_Republic "Grand Army of the Republic"), passed [a bill granting pensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_and_Disability_Pension_Act "Dependent and Disability Pension Act") for disabilities not caused by military service, Cleveland also vetoed that.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-122) In his first term alone, Cleveland used the veto 414 times, which was more than four times more often than any previous president had used it.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-123) In 1887, Cleveland issued his most well-known veto, that of the [Texas Seed Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Seed_Bill "Texas Seed Bill").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins331-124) After a drought had ruined crops in several Texas counties, Congress appropriated $100,000 (equivalent to $3,583,333 in 2025) to purchase seed grain for farmers there.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins331-124) Cleveland vetoed the expenditure. In his veto message, he espoused a theory of limited government:

> I can find no warrant for such an appropriation in the Constitution, and I do not believe that the power and duty of the general government ought to be extended to the relief of individual suffering which is in no manner properly related to the public service or benefit. A prevalent tendency to disregard the limited mission of this power and duty should, I think, be steadfastly resisted, to the end that the lesson should be constantly enforced that, though the people support the government, the government should not support the people. The friendliness and charity of our countrymen can always be relied upon to relieve their fellow-citizens in misfortune. This has been repeatedly and quite lately demonstrated. Federal aid in such cases encourages the expectation of paternal care on the part of the government and weakens the sturdiness of our national character, while it prevents the indulgence among our people of that kindly sentiment and conduct which strengthens the bonds of a common brotherhood.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-125)

### Silver

One of the most volatile issues of the 1880s was whether the currency should be backed by [gold and silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimetallism "Bimetallism"), or by [gold alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard "Gold standard").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-126) The issue cut across party lines, with Western Republicans and Southern Democrats joining in the call for the free coinage of silver, and both parties' representatives in the northeast holding firm for the gold standard.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins201-127) Because silver was worth less than its legal equivalent in gold, taxpayers paid their government bills in silver, while international creditors demanded payment in gold, resulting in a depletion of the nation's gold supply.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins201-127)

Cleveland and Treasury Secretary [Daniel Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Manning "Daniel Manning") stood firmly on the side of the gold standard, and tried to reduce the amount of silver that the government was required to coin under the [Bland–Allison Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bland%E2%80%93Allison_Act "Bland–Allison Act") of 1878.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-128) Cleveland unsuccessfully appealed to Congress to repeal this law before he was inaugurated.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-129) Angered Westerners and Southerners advocated for cheap money to help their poorer constituents.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-130) In reply, one of the foremost silverites, [Richard P. Bland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_P._Bland "Richard P. Bland"), introduced a bill in 1886 that would require the government to coin unlimited amounts of silver, inflating the then-deflating currency.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins273-131) While Bland's bill was defeated, so was a bill the administration favored that would repeal any silver coinage requirement.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins273-131) The result was a retention of the _status quo_, and a postponement of the resolution of the free-silver issue.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-132)

### Tariffs

"When we consider that the theory of our institutions guarantees to every citizen the full enjoyment of all the fruits of his industry and enterprise, with only such deduction as may be his share toward the careful and economical maintenance of the Government which protects him, it is plain that the exaction of more than this is indefensible extortion and a culpable betrayal of American fairness and justice... The public Treasury, which should only exist as a conduit conveying the people's tribute to its legitimate objects of expenditure, becomes a hoarding place for money needlessly withdrawn from trade and the people's use, thus crippling our national energies, suspending our country's development, preventing investment in productive enterprise, threatening financial disturbance, and inviting schemes of public plunder."
_**Cleveland's third annual message to Congress**,  
December 6, 1887._[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-133)

Another contentious financial issue at the time was the protective [tariff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff "Tariff"). These tariffs had been implemented as a temporary measure during the civil war to protect American industrial interests but remained in place after the war.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-134) While it had not been a central point in his campaign, Cleveland's opinion on the tariff was that of most Democrats: that the tariff ought to be reduced.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins280-135) Republicans generally favored a high tariff to protect American industries.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-nevins280-135) American tariffs had been high since the Civil War, and by the 1880s the tariff brought in so much revenue that the government was running a surplus.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-136)

In 1886, a bill to reduce the tariff was narrowly defeated in the House.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-137)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-138) The tariff issue was emphasized in [the Congressional elections that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1886_United_States_House_elections "1886 United States House elections"), and the forces of protectionism increased their numbers in the Congress, but Cleveland continued to advocate tariff reform.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-139) As the surplus grew, Cleveland and the reformers called for a tariff for revenue only.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-140) His message to Congress in 1887 (quoted at right) highlighted the injustice of taking more money from the people than the government needed to pay its operating expenses.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-141) Republicans, as well as protectionist northern Democrats like [Samuel J. Randall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_J._Randall "Samuel J. Randall"), believed that American industries would fail without high tariffs, and they continued to fight reform efforts.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-142)[Roger Q. Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Q._Mills "Roger Q. Mills"), chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, proposed a bill to reduce the tariff from about 47% to about 40%.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff88-143) After significant exertions by Cleveland and his allies, the bill passed the House but not the Senate.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff88-143)

### Foreign policy, 1885–1889

Cleveland was a committed [noninterventionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolationism "Isolationism") who had campaigned in opposition to expansion and imperialism. He refused to promote the previous administration's [Nicaragua canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_canal "Nicaragua canal") treaty, and generally was less of an expansionist in foreign relations.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-144) Cleveland's Secretary of State, [Thomas F. Bayard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_F._Bayard "Thomas F. Bayard"), negotiated with [Joseph Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Chamberlain "Joseph Chamberlain") of the United Kingdom over fishing rights in the waters off Canada, and struck a conciliatory note, despite the opposition of [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England")'s Republican Senators.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-145) Cleveland also withdrew from Senate consideration of the [Berlin Conference treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Conference "Berlin Conference") which guaranteed an open door for U.S. interests in [the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Free_State "Congo Free State").[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-wealth-146)

### Military and naval policy, 1885–1889

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Grover_Cleveland_by_Charles_Milton_Bell_color_change_%28b%26w%29.jpg/250px-Grover_Cleveland_by_Charles_Milton_Bell_color_change_%28b%26w%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grover_Cleveland_by_Charles_Milton_Bell_color_change_(b&w).jpg)

Cleveland in 1888

Cleveland's military policy emphasized self-defense and modernization. In 1885 Cleveland appointed the [Board of Fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Fortifications "Board of Fortifications") under [Secretary of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_War "Secretary of War")[William C. Endicott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Crowninshield_Endicott "William Crowninshield Endicott") to recommend a new [coastal fortification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seacoast_defense_in_the_United_States "Seacoast defense in the United States") system for the United States.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-Berhow,_pp._9-10-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-cdsg.org-148) No improvements to U.S. coastal defenses had been made since the late 1870s.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-149)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-150) The Board's 1886 report recommended a massive $127 million construction program (equivalent to $4.6 billion in 2025) at 29 [harbors and river estuaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbor_Defense_Command "Harbor Defense Command"), to include new breech-loading rifled guns, mortars, and [naval minefields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_mines_in_United_States_harbor_defense "Submarine mines in United States harbor defense"). The Board and the program are usually called the Endicott Board and the Endicott Program. Most of the Board's recommendations were implemented, and by 1910, 27 locations were defended by over 70 forts.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-151)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-152) Many of the weapons remained in place until scrapped in World War II as they were replaced with new defenses. Endicott also proposed to Congress a system of examinations for Army officer promotions.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-153) For the Navy, the Cleveland administration, spearheaded by [Secretary of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Navy "Secretary of the Navy")[William Collins Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Collins_Whitney "William Collins Whitney"), moved towards modernization, although no ships were constructed that could match the best European warships. Although completion of the four steel-hulled warships begun under the previous administration was delayed due to a corruption investigation and subsequent bankruptcy of their building yard, these ships were completed in a timely manner in [naval shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_shipyard "Naval shipyard") once the investigation was over.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-154) Sixteen additional steel-hulled warships were ordered by the end of 1888. These ships played a vital role during the [Spanish–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War "Spanish–American War") of 1898, and many later served in World War I. Among them were the "second-class [battleships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship "Battleship")" [_Maine_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Maine_(1890) "USS Maine (1890)") and [_Texas_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Texas_(1892) "USS Texas (1892)"), designed to match modern armored ships recently acquired by South American countries from Europe, such as the [Brazilian battleship _Riachuelo_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_battleship_Riachuelo "Brazilian battleship Riachuelo").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-155) Eleven [protected cruisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_cruiser "Protected cruiser") (including the famous [_Olympia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Olympia_(C-6) "USS Olympia (C-6)")), one [armored cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armored_cruiser "Armored cruiser"), and one [monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monitor_(warship) "Monitor (warship)") were also ordered, along with the experimental cruiser [_Vesuvius_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Vesuvius_(1888) "USS Vesuvius (1888)").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-156)

### Civil rights and immigration

Under Cleveland, gains in civil rights for African Americans were limited.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-157) Like a growing number of Northerners and nearly all white Southerners, he saw [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era") as a failed experiment,[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-158) and was reluctant to use federal power to enforce the [15th Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") of the [U.S. Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Constitution "U.S. Constitution"), which guaranteed voting rights to African Americans.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch65-159) Cleveland appointed no black Americans to patronage jobs, but allowed [Frederick Douglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass "Frederick Douglass") to continue in his post as [recorder of deeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recorder_of_deeds "Recorder of deeds") in Washington, D.C., and appointed another black man ([James Campbell Matthews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Campbell_Matthews "James Campbell Matthews"), a former New York judge) to replace Douglass upon his resignation.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch65-159) His decision to replace Douglass with a black man was met with outrage, but Cleveland claimed to have known Matthews personally.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-160)

Although Cleveland had condemned the "outrages" against Chinese immigrants, he believed that Chinese immigrants were unwilling to [assimilate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_assimilation "Cultural assimilation") into white society.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-161) Secretary of State Thomas F. Bayard negotiated an extension to the [Chinese Exclusion Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Exclusion_Act "Chinese Exclusion Act"), and Cleveland lobbied the Congress to pass the [Scott Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Act_(1888) "Scott Act (1888)"), written by Congressman [William Lawrence Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lawrence_Scott "William Lawrence Scott"), which prevented the return of Chinese immigrants who left the United States.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch73-162) The Scott Act easily passed both houses of Congress, and Cleveland signed it into law on October 1, 1888.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch73-162)

### Native American policy

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/HenryLDawes.jpg/250px-HenryLDawes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HenryLDawes.jpg)

[Henry L. Dawes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_L._Dawes "Henry L. Dawes") wrote the [Dawes Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Act "Dawes Act"), which Cleveland signed into law.

Cleveland viewed Native Americans as [wards of the state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wards_of_the_state "Wards of the state"), saying in his first inaugural address that "[t]his guardianship involves, on our part, efforts for the improvement of their condition and enforcement of their rights."[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch70-163) He encouraged the idea of cultural assimilation, pushing for the passage of the [Dawes Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes_Act "Dawes Act"), which would allow lands held in trust by the federal government for the tribes to instead be distributed to individual tribe members.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch70-163) While a conference of Native leaders endorsed the act, in practice the majority of Native Americans disapproved of it.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-164) Cleveland believed the Dawes Act would lift Native Americans out of poverty and encourage their assimilation into white society. It ultimately weakened the tribal governments and allowed individual Native Americans to sell land and keep the money.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-welch70-163) The act led to Native Americans ceding control of about 100 million acres of land between 1887 and 1934, which was around "two-thirds of the land base they held in 1887."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:7-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:8-7)

In the month before Cleveland's 1885 inauguration, President Arthur opened four million acres of [Ho-Chunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho-Chunk "Ho-Chunk") and [Crow Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crow_Creek_Indian_Reservation "Crow Creek Indian Reservation") lands in the [Dakota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_Territory "Dakota Territory") to white settlement by executive order.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-B141-165) Tens of thousands of settlers gathered at the border of these lands and prepared to take possession of them.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-B141-165) Cleveland believed Arthur's order to be in violation of treaties with the tribes, and rescinded it on April 17 of that year, ordering the settlers out of the territory.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-B141-165) Cleveland sent in eighteen [companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_(military_unit) "Company (military unit)") of Army troops to enforce the treaties and ordered General [Philip Sheridan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sheridan "Philip Sheridan"), at the time Commanding General of the U.S. Army, to investigate the matter.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-B141-165)

### Marriage and children

Main article: [Wedding of Grover Cleveland and Frances Folsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_of_Grover_Cleveland_and_Frances_Folsom "Wedding of Grover Cleveland and Frances Folsom")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Frances_Folsom_Cleveland.jpg/250px-Frances_Folsom_Cleveland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frances_Folsom_Cleveland.jpg)

Frances Folsom Cleveland, c.1886

Cleveland was 47 years old when he entered the White House as a bachelor. His sister [Rose Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Cleveland "Rose Cleveland") joined him, acting as hostess for the first 15 months of his administration.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-166) Unlike the previous bachelor president [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"), Cleveland did not remain a bachelor for long. In 1885, the daughter of Cleveland's friend Oscar Folsom visited him in Washington.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff78-167)[Frances Folsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Cleveland "Frances Cleveland") was a student at [Wells College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_College "Wells College"). When she returned to school, President Cleveland received her mother's permission to correspond with her, and they were soon engaged to be married.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-graff78-167) The [wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_of_Grover_Cleveland_and_Frances_Folsom "Wedding of Grover Cleveland and Frances Folsom") occurred on June 2, 1886, in the [Blue Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Room_(White_House) "Blue Room (White House)") at the White House. Cleveland was 49 years old at the time; Frances was 21.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-168) He was the second president to wed while in office[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-169) and remains the only president to marry in the White House. This marriage was unusual because Cleveland was the executor of Oscar Folsom's estate and had supervised Frances's upbringing after her father's death; nevertheless, the public took no exception to the match.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-170) At 21 years, Frances Folsom Cleveland was and remains the youngest [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States") in history, and soon became popular for her warm personality.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-171)

The Clevelands had five children: [Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Cleveland "Ruth Cleveland") (1891–1904), [Esther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esther_Cleveland "Esther Cleveland") (1893–1980), Marion (1895–1977), [Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_F._Cleveland "Richard F. Cleveland") (1897–1974), and [Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Cleveland "Francis Cleveland") (1903–1995). British philosopher [Philippa Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_Foot "Philippa Foot") (1920–2010) was their granddaughter.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-172) Ruth contracted [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria") on January 2, 1904, and died five days after her diagnosis.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-Quinn-173) The [Curtiss Candy Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss_Candy_Company "Curtiss Candy Company") would later assert that the "[Baby Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Ruth "Baby Ruth")" candy bar was named after her.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-174) Cleveland also claimed paternity of a child with Maria Crofts Halpin, [Oscar Folsom Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Folsom_Cleveland "Oscar Folsom Cleveland"), who was born in 1874.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland#cite_note-:9-54)
